To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the approximation by Peacock & Heaven for the first crossing problem with correlated steps can be interpreted as a correction to a smooth completely correlated random walk; (ii) the same correction can be applied to the case of walks constrained to pass through an arbitrary fixed point; (iii) the correction to the smooth completely correlated walk is independent of the barrier profile, as is also the correction for the walks with a fixed point.

the first crossing distribution for a barrier of constant height can be accurately approximated using smooth completely correlated random walks; and that the conditional first crossing distribution for walks that are forced to pass through a point can be accurately approximating by rescaling the unconditional first crossing by a bivariate Gaussian factor.

(i) the approximation of Peacock and Heavens is a correction to the first crossing distribution associated with smooth completely correlated walks, (ii) this approximation is valid for both constant and moving barriers and (iii) the unconditional distribution can be rescaled to obtain the conditional distribution.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the excursion set approach can be extended in a number of interesting ways, and that it provides accurate results for quantities of interest in the study of non-linear structure formation.

a simple prescription for the first crossing problem with correlated steps can be obtained by a rescaling of the unconditional first-crossing distribution, which is accurate for a broad class of barriers, and is applicable even in the presence of a stochastic barrier.

, for the first crossing distributions of interest to us, it is the correlation structure of the underlying Gaussian field rather than its stochastic nature that determines the form of the first crossing distribution, and that the stochasticity can be incorporated in a relatively simple way.
